back: $\mathrm{Var}(w)=2/n_{in}$, i.e. std $\sqrt{2/n_{in}}$, for ReLU. The 2 compensates for ReLU zeroing half the units.
$\mathrm{Var}(w)=2/(n_{in}+n_{out})$: a compromise between forward and backward variance preservation, for roughly linear activations (tanh).

front: Symptom of Xavier init with ReLU
back: The second moment halves each layer; in the lesson measurement the std fell to $10^{-8}$ after 50 layers.

front: Why not initialise all weights to zero?
back: Symmetry: every unit in a layer computes and receives the same thing and stays identical.

front: Cheap diagnostics to log per layer
back: Activation mean/std, fraction of exact zeros, gradient norm. Vanishing: tiny early-layer norms; exploding: nan/inf or growth.
$\hat x=(x-\mu_B)/\sqrt{\sigma_B^2+\varepsilon}$, $y=\gamma\hat x+\beta$; statistics per feature over the batch.
$\bar x=\frac{\mathrm{inv}}{N}\big(N\bar{\hat x}-\sum\bar{\hat x}-\hat x\sum\bar{\hat x}\hat x\big)$ with $\bar{\hat x}=\bar y\gamma$.
Use running averages of mean and variance collected in training (exponential average, momentum about 0.1); no batch dependence.
Depends on batch statistics: noisy for small batches, meaningless for $N=1$, train/eval mismatch.
Normalise each example over its $D$ features: same in train and eval, any batch size. Backward: same formula with sums over features and $N\to D$.
$y=\gamma x/\sqrt{\frac1D\sum x^2+\varepsilon}$: no mean subtraction, no shift. Used in LLaMA-style models.

front: Properties of the batch-norm input gradient
back: Sums to zero over the batch and is orthogonal to $\hat x$: invariance to shifting and scaling the inputs.
